item.title: Slovakia's Biology Olympiad: It Only Gets Easier
item.description:
Daniel Jediný

🥉 IBO 2026 Bronze Medallist · Slovakia 🇸🇰

Daniel is an IBO 2026 bronze medallist from Slovakia and a student at Univerzita Komenského v Bratislave (Comenius University) -- the same university that hosts Slovakia's national IBO selection camp. Connect with him on LinkedIn.

Slovakia’s Biology Olympiad – it only gets easier

"As one of the founding countries of IBO, Slovakia's national Bio Olympiad still keeps close to what one might expect on an international level. Except... not really. Whilst you can expect the national round to feel somewhat similar, the Slovak biology Olympiad consist of three rounds, starting as a purely knowledge-based competition, that keeps slowly transforming into something closer to the IBO. It starts to reward logical thinking over just remembering information, which is ever more true for the selection camp."

"That being said, if you give it your all for the first (school) round already, it will only get easier from there, requiring significantly less extra study, the further you get."

"So go get your IBO medal! If you have that dawg in you, that is 😉."

The official picture

Daniel’s account lines up with how Slovakia’s Ministry of Education, Science, Research and Sports describes the Biologická Olympiáda officially. The competition dates back to 1963, with Iuventa (the Slovak Institute of Youth) appointed to organise it and the Slovak Committee of Biology Olympiad handling the scientific content:

RoundTimingFormat
SchoolFebruaryKnowledge-based theory, school-level entry point
RegionalMarchTheory (multiple choice and short answer) plus two practical tasks per student -- dissection, physiological, or biochemical experiments
NationalAprilSame format as regional, at higher difficulty; roughly 300-350 students reach this stage

From there, the top 10-12 students from the national round enter two selection weeks – one theory-focused, one practical – held at Slovak universities, typically Comenius University in Bratislava (where Daniel now studies) or the Slovak University of Agriculture in Nitra. The best six – four competitors and two backups – are selected to represent Slovakia. This is the stage Daniel describes as rewarding “logical thinking over just remembering information”: it is a genuinely different kind of test from the school round that starts the whole process.

Sources: IBO country profile – Biologická Olympiáda, Slovakia.

IBO prep and BiOGuide, in his own words

Find resources easily

"One of the main challenges when studying for IBO is actually not the study itself. That would be resource hunting! Whilst just knowing all the topics you need to learn might pose a challenge to some, it is even harder to find sources which are detailed enough to meet your needs, without needlessly hyperspecializing in the topic. Bioguide acts as a large library of precisely such sources gathered for IBO participants by the IBO participants."

Avoid wasting your time

"Did you know that most IBO participants are more likely to regret having studied a particular topic rather than not having studied one? It is well known, that IBO prep is no simple task, and with hoards of topics to study it can be hard to pick the right ones to focus on. That is the main benefit of BioGuide. Although randomly self-studied knowledge might still prove useful, no matter how obscene the topic, it is way more likely to just cost you time you could be putting in, where it matters."

Practice makes perfect

"Although knowledge is a big part of what's being tested on IBO, it's by far not the only thing. It is just as important to be able to think within the context of information provided, as well as your general medical knowledge. So use BioGuide's archive of past years exams and practice, practice, practice!"

How BiOGuide fits in

Daniel’s three points map onto specific things BiOGuide is built to do:

  • His “large library of precisely such sources” is Notes @ BiOGuide – topic pages written to be detailed enough for IBO-level prep without sprawling into needless hyperspecialization, organised so a student can find the exact concept they need rather than hunting across scattered sources.

  • Not wasting time on the wrong topics is what the Study Dashboard is for – after a timed attempt, it builds a subject-by-subject mastery breakdown and ranks what to study next, so effort goes toward genuinely weak areas rather than whatever topic happens to catch your attention.

  • “Practice, practice, practice” is BiOrchive, the archive of past IBO papers, and the Question Bank underneath it – every question carries the topics it draws on, so practice can be targeted at exactly the kind of contextual, apply-the-information thinking Daniel describes IBO actually testing.

This article preserves Daniel’s own words, shared and published with his consent. If you competed in a Biology Olympiad and want to share your story, reach out to us – we would love to hear from you.

item.title: Azerbaijan's Olympiad structure and BiOGuide relevance
item.description:
Huseyn Taghizada

IRBO and AZ NTBO Merit Holder · Azerbaijan 🇦🇿

Hello there. I am Huseyn Taghizada, biology olympiadist from Azerbaijan. I will not talk about neither my medals nor anything other. You can check them from my linkedin account with the same name. Relying on my experiences my main goal is guide students thorough this harsh olympiad path and finishing it with the best possible ending. If you're interested in my hobbies they're quite lot in fact. Chess, books, films, music, mangas and much more. Feel free to contact me via huseyntagizade90@gmail.com.

Azerbaijan’s Republic Biology Olympiad, in his own words

Huseyn put together a full walkthrough of the biology category of Azerbaijan’s national olympiad – the Respublika Fənn Olimpiadaları, or RFO – for anyone in his country considering the same path:

"RFO is an olympiad that gather students from every part of country. Unfortunely for Biology category our school biology curriculum has nothing to do with National or International Olympiads. So you can assume that if we decide to step on Olympiad journey, we start from absolute scratch."

"RFO consists of mainly 3 rounds (yet sometimes it can be 4 which means you have to pass school round to participate in next rounds, but it is not that important so i will not refer something about school round): District-city round, Semifinal, Final."

"First round or City round most likely requires essential biology knowledges. Just taking a look at Campbell would be more than enough for it. This round contains only multiple-choice questions whose number do not pass 20 or 25."

"Next Round is Semifinal in which Students are going to need much more knowledge and problem solving skill. Reading and learning all the topics from Campbell required. For solving questions much more easily student should look at or analyze IBO questions. This round contains only multiple-choice questions either. Consists of 25-30 questions."

"Last Round or Final round. Final round divided into 2 parts: Theoretical and Practical. Theoretical round contains IBO level questions for short period of time which requires time management skills. For this round Student should read from different kinds of sources. In case instances are needed some of them are Sherwood Physiology or Alberts Essential Cell Biology. Question count is incostintent so I can not tell exact count but range is between 15-25. All of the questions are IBO type: True/False, Calculation problems or drawing problems (phylogenic tree)."

"For practical round I have not much of word to say because it was started being helded only for 2 years. One of them was TLC and other one was Fish dissection. I am looking forward for bringing varieties to this section."

The official picture

Huseyn’s account matches how Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Education describes the competition officially:

RoundTimingFormat
District-cityJanuaryMultiple-choice, school-curriculum level; students need roughly 60% correct to advance
SemifinalMarchMultiple-choice, IBO-adjacent difficulty
Final (Theoretical + Practical)MayIBO-style True/False, calculation, and drawing questions; practical stations (added in the last two years) have so far covered TLC and fish dissection

The whole programme runs under the Ministry of Education of the Republic of Azerbaijan, hosted by the Institute of Education of the Republic of Azerbaijan, and dates back to 1993. Around 2,000-2,500 students sit the first round each year, and winners of the final round are awarded gold, silver, or bronze medals along with guaranteed university entrance to a biology programme in Azerbaijan without a separate entrance exam.

Sources: IBO country profile – Republican Biology Olympiad, Azerbaijan.

How BiOGuide fits in

Huseyn’s own description of RFO maps closely onto how the three rounds actually escalate in difficulty, and that escalation is exactly what BiOGuide’s structure is built to support:

  • Notes @ BiOGuide covers the syllabus at the depth Huseyn points students toward for the Semifinal and Final rounds – the same territory as Campbell, Sherwood, and Alberts, organised by topic so a student can go straight to the concept they’re missing instead of a full chapter.

  • BiOrchive, the archive of past IBO papers, is the natural next step once a student reaches the point Huseyn describes – needing to “look at or analyze IBO questions” to prepare for the Semifinal, and needing genuine IBO-level time management for the Final’s theoretical round. Every question in the archive’s Question Bank is topic-tagged, so practice can be targeted rather than random.

  • The Study Dashboard turns timed practice attempts into a mastery breakdown by topic, which is useful for exactly the kind of self-directed, starting-from-scratch preparation Huseyn describes for students without a curriculum overlap to lean on.

As Huseyn put it himself: “BioGuide will play key role in students Olympiad life. It will not only guide him/her for nationals but also afterwards for IBO or other international Olympiads. Most of the resources you recommended are absolutely necessary for RFO and of course for selection for IBO team.”

This article preserves Huseyn’s own words, shared and published with his consent. “As I said earlier I am appreciating you and your team for this awesome and beneficial project and slowly being part of it is my honor.” If you competed in a Biology Olympiad and want to share your story, reach out to us – we would love to hear from you.

item.title: From Belgium to IBO Bronze: Jonas's Story
item.description:
Jonas Wulleman

🥉 IBO 2026 Bronze Medallist · Belgium 🇧🇪

Hi there! I'm Jonas from Belgium. I participated at the IBO 2026 in Vilnius, Lithuania, and got a bronze medal🥉. I am also very interested in other science disciplines, and especially mathematics and physics, which I will study at university next year. I have also competed in math olympiads, f.e. the EMC or BxMO, which were my first contact with young scientists from other countries 😊. I also love music, I play the piano (and a bit of cello), and have Finnish roots (do you know Jean Sibelius? He is a famous composer from Finland!).

In his own words

Hi everyone 👋

As an IBO 2026 participant and bronze medallist from Belgium, I would have been thrilled if this site had existed when I participated! During our training programme, there was not much emphasis on getting familiar with the types of questions asked at the IBO theory exams. Most of the theoretical preparation was also largely left to us as self-study, which made it quite challenging to know what to focus on.

The fact that BioGuide has an archive containing many past IBO theory questions, accompanied by model solutions, is incredibly helpful. I also find it extremely useful that you can see which theoretical concepts are necessary to solve each question. This really is a lifesaver when you don't have much time to prepare for the IBO.

Furthermore, the interactive part of the site, where you can identify which domains are still most challenging for you, comes in very handy. In Belgium, we only have one or two hours of biology a week, so our knowledge can be quite limited compared to other countries. Personally, I have always found more challenging problems on genetic recombination particularly difficult. That's why the mini-courses on the site are so convenient: they explain everything clearly, without having to search through the entire Campbell to find the relevant information.

I hope this site will help fellow Belgian students, as well as students from all around the world, to prepare for the IBO and arrive at the starting line confidently! But the most important thing remains: have fun and enjoy the ride! The IBO is truly something you will never experience again 🍀

Belgium’s two biology olympiads

Belgium’s setup for biology olympiad selection is fairly unusual, and Jonas explained it best in his own words:

"The thing is, in Belgium we have 2 bio-olympiads: 1 for the Dutch-speaking community and 1 for the French-speaking community. Both olympiads are conducted independently from each other, so I have only info about the Dutch-speaking organization."

"Also, our 1st and 2nd round (in both country parts) are really only based on the things we learn at schools. BioGuide is a bit too high-level for our 1st en 2nd round (even final), so the site is more suited for the people who actually go to the IBO to prepare"

This is a useful distinction if you are a Belgian student reading this: the early rounds of both the Dutch-speaking and French-speaking olympiads test school-level content, and BiOGuide’s syllabus-depth material genuinely is more than that stage calls for. Where it earns its place, per Jonas, is in the narrower and more intense window between qualifying for the international stage and actually sitting the IBO theory exam.

The official picture

Jonas’s description matches how both organisations describe themselves officially. Belgium’s four-student IBO team is drawn from two olympiads that run completely independently of each other, one per language community:

Vlaamse Biologie Olympiade (VBO) Olympiade de Biologie
Community Dutch-speaking (Flanders) French- and German-speaking
Organiser VOB vzw (biology teachers’ association), coordinated through Vlaamse Olympiades voor Natuurwetenschappen at KU Leuven PROBIO asbl (biology teachers’ association)
Established 1990 1991
Round 1 January - 25 MCQs, 2 hours, at schools (~2,300 students) January - at schools (~1,000 students); ~100-200 advance
Round 2 February/early March - 30 MCQs, 2 hours, at Flemish universities (~200 students) February - at five regional university sites; ~10-15 laureates per grade
Final round April - 40-question theory paper (2.5 h) plus a two-part practical exam, for 17 finalists at a rotating host university May - grade-12-only round that sets the final ranking
IBO selection Top 2 finalists represent Belgium Top 2 finalists represent Belgium
Official site vob-ond.be/VBO olympiades.be

Belgium’s IBO team of four is therefore always two Flemish-selected students plus two French/German-community-selected students, chosen through entirely separate qualification pipelines that never overlap until the students meet as teammates at the IBO itself.

Sources: IBO country profile - Vlaamse Biologie Olympiade, IBO country profile - Olympiade de Biologie.

How BiOGuide fits in

Jonas’s account lines up closely with three specific things BiOGuide is built to do:

  • BiOrchive, the archive of past IBO theory papers, is what he means by “an archive containing many past IBO theory questions, accompanied by model solutions.” Every question in the archive’s Question Bank also carries the syllabus topics it draws on, so instead of just checking an answer, you can trace a question back to exactly what to review - the “you can see which theoretical concepts are necessary to solve each question” he called out directly.

  • The Study Dashboard is the “interactive part of the site” he’s describing. After a timed attempt, it builds a subject-by-subject mastery breakdown and tells you plainly which domains are strongest and which need work - useful for anyone, but especially so for a student getting one or two hours of biology instruction a week at school and needing every hour of outside study time to count.

  • Notes @ BiOGuide is the “mini-courses” he mentions. Genetic recombination - the specific topic he named as a persistent sticking point - has its own dedicated page under the Genetics section, built to explain the concept directly rather than send you hunting through a full textbook chapter for the two paragraphs that matter.

None of this replaces a dedicated coach or a full national training programme. But for students in systems like Belgium’s, where the international stage is reached with comparatively little formal preparation beforehand, having a free, structured resource to close that gap can matter a great deal.

item.title: From Turkmenistan to IBO: How 6 Students Are Using BiOGuide
item.description:
The challenge

Turkmenistan has sent teams to the International Biology Olympiad for years, but results have been difficult. No Turkmen student has brought home a medal in the past two IBO cycles - not for lack of talent or drive, but for a reason that may be familiar to some smaller delegations: the students have been using the self-studying technique and passing their knowledge down the generations by their own selves without proper guidance over years.

The technique that Meryem, her partners, and previous IBO competitors from the past two years have been using is something remarkable in its own way: older students who have been through the process pass what they know to younger ones. The team is largely self-taught, built on a culture of peer mentoring where each generation tries to leave the next one a little better prepared than they were.

But self-study has limits. Resources are hard to come by. Structured programmes in English-language biology olympiad preparation are rare, and the ones that exist often carry a price tag that puts them out of reach. Turkmenistan’s biology olympiad students have been making do with whatever they can find - scattered PDFs, secondhand textbooks, and advice from alumni who graduated years ago.

Turkmenistan’s national biology olympiad

The self-directed, peer-taught approach Meryem’s team relies on makes more sense once you see how the national pathway is actually built. The Turkmen National Biology Olympiad, run by the Ministry of Education of Turkmenistan since 1995, is a four-round funnel: it starts at school level, where roughly 1,000 students sit the first round and the top 2-3 from each school advance; then district level, where the top 3 move on; then regional level, again narrowing to the top 3; and finally a national round, open only to 10th and 11th graders, hosted in a different city each year. Question formats vary round to round - multiple choice, problem solving, fill-in-the-blanks, picture-based questions, and occasionally oral components - set by the National Institute of Education together with Turkmen State University.

What the official structure does not provide is IBO-specific preparation material along the way - the rounds test and select, but nothing in the pipeline is built to teach students the IBO syllabus itself. That gap is exactly what Meryem’s team has been filling for each other, generation after generation, and exactly where a free structured resource has room to matter.

Source: IBO country profile - Turkmen National Biology Olympiad.

Why BiOGuide

Meryem, one of six students forming the core of Turkmenistan’s current preparation group, heard about BiOGuide’s one-year preparation programme and saw something that matched what her team needed:

  • It is completely free. Every resource, every guide, every practice paper - no paywalls, no premium tiers, no “free trial” that expires. For a team operating on limited means in a country where international subscriptions are not straightforward, this matters more than any single feature.

  • It is structured around the IBO syllabus. BiOGuide’s notes are organised into the same subject categories that IBO itself tests - Cell Biology, Animal Anatomy and Physiology, Genetics and Evolution, Plant Biology, Ecology, Ethology, and Biosystematics. Instead of hunting across ten different websites for scattered material on each topic, the team can follow a single pathway from start to finish.

  • The one-year study plan gives them a timeline. Self-study often fails not because the material is too hard, but because there is no pacing - no external structure saying “you should be here by November.” BiOGuide’s preparation guides lay out a month-by-month progression that gives the team a realistic schedule to follow, with enough flexibility to adapt to their own pace.

How the team is using it

The six students are working through BiOGuide’s resources together. Their approach:

Subject notes as the backbone. The members can fo through the Notes@BiOGuide section and read according to their own needs. Any subject, any relevant part. Name it and it is available. What books can’t provide, the notes section does. IBO resources compiled into one singular compressed and designated resource.

BiOrchive for practice. BiOGuide’s archive of past IBO papers with solutions gives the team something they previously struggled to find: real exam-level questions with worked answers. They are using these for timed practice sessions, simulating actual IBO conditions as closely as they can.

BiOClash for competitive preparation. When BiOClash rounds open, the individuals plan to participate and compete - not just for the scores, but for the experience of working under timed pressure on original biology problems. The subject-specific rounds align with the topics they are studying each month, giving them a natural checkpoint.

Discord for community. The BiOGuide Discord server connects them to students from dozens of other countries - people preparing for the same competition, facing similar challenges, and willing to share advice. For a team that has been largely isolated in their preparation, this is new and valuable.

What they hope to achieve

Meryem puts it simply: “We’d genuinely love to see how far we can take it.”

The goal is an IBO medal - but the ambition goes beyond that. If the programme works, the plan is to grow it: bring more Turkmenistan students into the fold, build a larger and more sustainable preparation pipeline, and break the cycle of each generation starting from scratch.

BiOGuide did not create their determination. What it offers is something they have not had before: a free, structured, syllabus-aligned programme that fits the way they already work - peer-driven, self-directed, and built on the belief that students who want to learn should not be held back by what they cannot afford.

This article was written with Meryem’s input and published with her consent. If you or your team would like to share your own story of preparing for a Biology Olympiad, reach out to us - we would love to hear from you.
